sections.body_md:
Gram-Schmidt turns an independent list into an orthogonal list, one vector at a time. The first vector is kept. From each later vector, subtract its projections onto the vectors already accepted. The remainder is orthogonal to every accepted vector. The coefficient of an accepted vector \(u\) in the new vector \(v\) is the inner product of \(v\) and \(u\), divided by the squared length of \(u\).

The same arithmetic belongs to any inner product. Only the meaning of the product and of the squared length changes. When the product is \(x^T Q y\) with \(Q\) symmetric positive definite, the squared length is \(x^T Q x\). The vectors that come out then satisfy \(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\). That relation is called \(Q\)-conjugacy. Positive definiteness is what makes the squared length positive for every nonzero vector, so the division is legal.

Independence is what keeps every remainder nonzero. A vector that already lies in the span of the accepted ones is reproduced exactly by its projections, and the remainder vanishes. A zero remainder is not a new direction.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With an accepted vector \(u\) and a new vector \(v\),
\[
c = \frac{\langle v, u\rangle}{\langle u, u\rangle}, \qquad w = v - c\, u.
\]
For the product \(x^T Q y\), both the numerator and the denominator use that product. Then \(w^T Q u = 0\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take the dot product, the first vector \((4,\ 0)\), and the next vector \((6,\ 8)\). The inner product is \(24\) and the squared length of the first vector is \(16\). The coefficient is \(24/16\).

The keel coefficient is 1.5. Subtracting \(1.5\) times \((4,\ 0)\) from \((6,\ 8)\) leaves \((0,\ 8)\). The dot product of \((4,\ 0)\) with \((0,\ 8)\) is \(0\), so the two results are orthogonal. Scaling the first result to unit length would multiply this zero by a constant and leave it zero.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Using the inner product itself as the coefficient skips the division by the squared length. That over-subtracts whenever the accepted vector is not a unit vector. A second slip is to subtract a multiple of the new vector instead of a multiple of the accepted one. A third is to feed an indefinite symmetric matrix into \(x^T Q y\) and still call the result an inner product. Some nonzero vector then has a negative squared length. A fourth is to expect a nonzero remainder from a dependent list. Dependence is the case in which some remainder is zero. A fifth is to project onto the original inputs after they have stopped being orthogonal. The coefficients use the orthogonal vectors already accepted.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A list with \(d_i^T Q d_j = 0\) is a conjugate set for the quadratic whose Hessian is \(Q\). Exact line search along a full conjugate set reaches the minimizer of that quadratic in finitely many steps. Conjugate gradient builds the same kind of directions from gradients, instead of orthogonalizing a list that was chosen in advance.
